These uses can often enhance your learning experience. However, AI tools must not replace your own
analysis, critical thinking, or academic writing.

With data safety and uniformity in mind, the TU Delft recommends using the web-version of Microsoft Copilot
at this moment in time. You can log into Copilot with your TU Delft credentials.


Student Responsibilities
As a student, you are ultimately responsible for your own work, including any work produced with the help of AI.

When using AI tools, be aware of the following responsibilities:


   •   Permission: Check the written statement* regarding AI use for

each course.
   •   Transparency: Always cite and describe your use of AI tools in accordance with the
       acknowledgment** text that your instructor decides upon.
   •   Critical Evaluation: AI outputs may be inaccurate, biased, or fabricated. You remain fully
       responsible for all submitted work.
   •   Academic integrity: You are expected to adhere to the principles of academic integrity, as outlined
       in the Code of Conduct.
   •   Safe use: Do not disclose personal or sensitive information. Be aware that AI plug-ins make the
       accidental disclosure of personal or sensitive information even easier.
   •   Environmental awareness: AI tools and software are taxing on the

environment. Consider
       sustainability and energy efficiency when using AI.
Currently, the Microsoft Copilot Chat (after logging in with NetID) is the only generative AI tool permitted for use at TU Delft for education.

Generative AI Guidelines for Students – Faculty of Mechanical Engineering



Generative AI tools (such as Copilot, ChatGPT, and Gemini) are rapidly changing how we study and work.
The following guideline outlines when and how students can use such tools within their education at the
Faculty of Mechanical Engineering, while ensuring academic integrity, personal learning, and ethical
responsibility.


AI as a Learning Support Tool

AI tools can support your learning by:
    • Explaining concepts
    • Refining language
    • Assisting with programming and debugging
    • Acting as a brainstorming partner


These uses can often enhance your learning experience. However, AI tools

must not replace your own
analysis, critical thinking, or academic writing.

With data safety and uniformity in mind, the TU Delft recommends using the web-version of Microsoft Copilot
at this moment in time. You can log into Copilot with your TU Delft credentials.


Student Responsibilities
As a student, you are ultimately responsible for your own work, including any work produced with the help of AI.

When using AI tools, be aware of the following responsibilities:


   •   Permission: Check the written statement* regarding AI use for each course.
   •   Transparency: Always cite and describe your use of AI tools in accordance with the
       acknowledgment** text that your instructor deci

des upon.
   •   Critical Evaluation: AI outputs may be inaccurate, biased, or fabricated. You remain fully
       responsible for all submitted work.
   •   Academic integrity: You are expected to adhere to the principles of academic integrity, as outlined
       in the Code of Conduct.
   •   Safe use: Do not disclose personal or sensitive information. Be aware that AI plug-ins make the
       accidental disclosure of personal or sensitive information even easier.
   •   Environmental awareness: AI tools and software are taxing on the environment. Consider
       sustainability and energy efficiency when using AI.




January 2026

Generative AI Guidelines for Students – Faculty of Mechanical Engineering


AI use in unsupervised assessment

With Student Responsibility (page 1) in mind, the rule of thumb regarding AI use is 'Yes, unless'.

Your instructor will inform you via a written statement* about any restricted or prohibited uses of AI in
their course.

For certain assignments or course elements, instructors may discourage, restrict, or prohibit the use of AI
tools. If this is the case, you are required to add an acknowledgement** to your work.

Your instructor might limit the use of AI if they feel it conflicts with the learning objectives of the course.

If your instructor imposes restrictions on t

he use of AI, communicates these via a written statement*,
and you do not use the acknowledgment** form in your work, this could be considered fraudulent.

Instance of fraudulent behaviour will be handled in accordance with the faculty's regulations:
Fraud C Plagiarism - Regulations (article 7).

If in doubt, always consult your instructor about prohibited or restricted use of AI tools in coursework.

evidence.evidenceSnippet: Relying on AI-detection tools to penalise students risks false accusations, unfair treatment, and a breakdown of trust between staff and students. While plagiarism checkers help enforce clear rules, AI detectors operate in a grey area where “false positives” are common and untestable. Using them as a policing mechanism is therefore neither effective nor equitable in way of upholding assessment integrity. Instead, it is recommended that educators focus on adapting assessments to be more AI-resilient.

a useful ally in this regard. Plagiarism checkers compare student work against vast databases of existing text and are generally reliable at identifying direct copying.
By contrast, AI-detection tools attempt to judge whether a piece of text has been generated by AI, which is inherently more difficult to verify. Research has shown that these tools are often inaccurate and can drive students to adopt basic “evasion” prompting techniques that further reduce their accuracy (Liang et al., 2024).
